title: Canadian household spending recovered unevenly: shelter and food remain concentrated while recreation, restaurants, and travel reopen through unequal household room
source_unit: Statistics Canada, Survey of Household Spending 2023, updated September 18, 2026 with 2021-Census-calibrated weights
geography: Canada; provinces and the three territorial capitals, with income-quintile, household-type, tenure, and provincial comparisons

observations.period: 2023 reference year; updated September 18, 2026; national expenditure composition

denominator.unit: sample households: 9,991 households in the provinces and 732 in the three territorial capitals

total_goods_services.unit: average annual current-dollar spending on goods and services per Canadian household

shelter_share.unit: percent of total consumption allocated to shelter

transport_share.unit: percent of total consumption allocated to transportation

food_share.unit: percent of total consumption allocated to food

food_total.unit: average annual food spending per household, including stores and restaurants

restaurant_food.unit: average annual spending on food purchased from restaurants

observations.method: Statistics Canada Survey of Household Spending, using household expenditure data and updated weights calibrated to demographic projections based on the 2021 Census; estimates are current dollars and include sales taxes.
observations.uncertainty: Average spending is not a median or household welfare measure and is not inflation-adjusted. The survey covers the provinces for Canada-level estimates and the three territorial capitals separately; category averages include households with and without expenditures in the category.
observations.subgroup: Canadian households, provinces, and territorial capitals.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher nominal spending can reflect inflation, household composition, or reopening after pandemic restrictions rather than improved real purchasing power or cultural participation.

observations.period: 2019-2023 reference years; updated September 18, 2026; post-pandemic cultural and social consumption

denominator.unit: SHS sample households across provinces and the three territorial capitals

recreation.unit: average annual recreation spending per household in 2023, up 23.9% from 2021

recreation_services_change.unit: percent increase from 2021 to 2023 in recreational services spending, including cinemas, live sport, performing arts, and package trips

accommodation_away.unit: average annual spending on accommodation away from home in 2023, up 129.2% from 2021

accommodation_vs_2019.value: 2023 accommodation spending surpassed the 2019 pre-pandemic level after a 44.9% decline from 2019 to 2021

personal_care.unit: average annual personal-care spending per household in 2023, up 30.1% from 2021

observations.method: Repeated reference-year comparisons from the SHS category tables; 2023 estimates use the refreshed 2021-Census-calibrated weights.
observations.uncertainty: The recovery pattern does not identify which households resumed participation, whether services were affordable, or whether spending represents durable cultural practice versus one-time reopening and price effects.
observations.subgroup: Canadian households by recreation, accommodation, personal-care, household type, income, tenure, and geography.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rebound in paid recreation and travel can coexist with material constraint if spending is concentrated among higher-income or already-connected households.

observations.period: 2023 reference year; income-quintile and household-type allocation

denominator.unit: SHS sample households; income groups are five equal population groups

top_bottom_total_gap.unit: average annual goods-and-services spending in the highest income quintile versus 40080 in the lowest quintile

lowest_quintile_shelter.unit: percent of total consumption allocated to shelter in the lowest income quintile

highest_quintile_shelter.unit: percent allocated to shelter in the highest income quintile

lowest_quintile_food.unit: percent allocated to food in the lowest income quintile

highest_quintile_recreation.unit: percent allocated to recreation in the highest income quintile versus 5.4% in the lowest quintile

one_person_shelter.unit: percent of total consumption allocated to shelter by one-person households

couple_no_children_recreation.unit: percent allocated to recreation by couples without children

observations.method: SHS estimates compared by income quintile and household type using the refreshed weights; spending shares are shares of total current consumption.
observations.uncertainty: Income quintile comparisons are descriptive and current-dollar; they do not estimate marginal propensities, price elasticity, debt, wealth, unpaid cultural participation, or causal effects of household composition.
observations.subgroup: Lowest and highest income quintiles, one-person households, couples with and without children, and other Canadian household types.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower recreation share may reflect necessity spending, household age, care responsibilities, or different free cultural practices rather than absence of cultural value.

Official table index linking household spending by income quintile, household type, tenure, geography, area size, age, and equipment.
Statistics Canada household-spending visualization tool for geography, tenure, household type, and income quintile comparisons.

boundary: This record adds an observed household-consumption and cultural-participation layer from Canada: essential spending concentration, reopening of restaurants, recreation, travel and personal care, and unequal household room by income and type. It uses current-dollar averages and refreshed survey weights; it is not real consumption, a panel, a causal welfare estimate, or evidence that paid spending captures all cultural participation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Statistics Canada September 18, 2026 release and table index were reviewed for refreshed weights, sample, category values, post-pandemic changes, income-quintile shares, household-type differences, geography, and current-dollar boundaries.
